title: Rabbi Yonatan (Rabbi Chiyya’s Student)
author: Aharon Hyman

paragraphs: Rabbi Yonatan (Rabbi Chiyya’s student). Hyman identifies him as a Babylonian and Rabbi Chiyya’s student, and states that he was not a Kohen, as in [Berakhot 18a](https://www.sefaria.org/Berakhot.18a.13): “Rabbi Chiyya and Rabbi Yonatan were walking in a cemetery; Rabbi Yonatan’s tekhelet was trailing.” This Rabbi Yonatan was the teacher of Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani, who always spoke in his name, [as it concludes there](https://www.sefaria.org/Berakhot.18b.17): Rabbi Yonatan, too, retracted. Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani reports the following in his name:

“From where [do we know] that the dead …?” In [Jerusalem Talmud Berakhot 2:3:15](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Berakhot.2.3.15): “Rabbi Chiyya Rova and Rabbi Yonatan went after the bier of Rabbi Shimon son of Rabbi Yose ben Lakonya, and Rabbi Yonatan was stepping over his grave,” etc.; and it is cited in Kohelet Rabbah 9:5: “Rabbi Chiyya Rabbah and Rabbi Yonatan were walking before the bier of Rabbi Shimon ben Yose ben Lakonya; Rabbi Yonatan’s tallit was trailing on his coffin. Rabbi Chiyya said to him: My son, lift your tallit …

He said to him: My teacher! Is it not written,” etc. In [Sanhedrin 71a:15](https://www.sefaria.org/Sanhedrin.71a.15): “Rabbi Yonatan said: I saw (a rebellious son) and sat on his grave.” He likewise kept company with Rabbi Chiyya, as in [Avodah Zarah 17a:17](https://www.sefaria.org/Avodah_Zarah.17a.17): “Rabbi Chiyya and Rabbi Yonatan were walking on the road; they came to those paths,” etc. This Rabbi Yonatan likewise received from Rabbi Shimon son of Rabbi Yose ben Lakonya, in Jerusalem Talmud Eruvin 3:4:

“Rabbi Yonatan said before Rabbi Chiyya Rova in the name of Rabbi Shimon son of Rabbi Yose ben Lakonya.” In Jerusalem Talmud Horayot 2:5 he asked him; in [Shevuot 18b:4](https://www.sefaria.org/Shevuot.18b.4) Hyman considers the saying to be cited in error.[^9] In [Bekhorot 38b](https://www.sefaria.org/Bekhorot.38b.5-7): Rabbah bar bar Chana recounts what Rabbi Yochanan told him: “There was an old man in our neighborhood, and Rabbi Shimon [ben] Lakonya was his name … he said to me: Sit, my son, sit,” etc. For the first name Hyman proposes Rabbah bar Chana; for the second, he cites Shitah Mekubbetzet’s Rabbi Yonatan.[^8]

He was a colleague of Rabbi Chanina, Rabbi Yannai and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, as in [Ketubot 49b:13](https://www.sefaria.org/Ketubot.49b.13): Rabbi Chanina and Rabbi Yannai were standing; a man came, bent down and kissed Rabbi Yonatan on his foot, and Rabbi Yonatan explained to Rabbi Chanina that he had compelled that man’s son to support the man. As in [Jerusalem Talmud Kiddushin 1:7:15](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Kiddushin.1.7.15), the incident is related as having been with Rabbi Yannai.[^10] In Taanit 2:12: “Rabbi Chanina and Rabbi Yonatan both say: Megillat Taanit has been annulled.”

In [Jerusalem Talmud Eruvin 6:4:5](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Eruvin.6.4.5): “Rabbi Chanina and Rabbi Yonatan went up to Chamat Gader; they said: Let us wait until the elders of the South come here. Rabbi Natan of the South came, and they asked him”; Hyman writes: I have already explained in his entry that it should read “Rabbi Pas of the South came,” and he is Rabbi Afes. In Kohelet Rabbah (locator supplied as פ״הדי; matching passage at 5:10): Rabbi Chanina and Rabbi Yonatan asked Menachem Talmia; and Rabbi Berekhyah in the name of Rabbi Yose son of Rabbi Chanina said that Menachem

Talmia asked them. In Jerusalem Talmud Maaser Sheni 3:3: Rabbi Chanina, Rabbi Yonatan and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi went up to Jerusalem; fruit came into their possession [נתמט], etc. In Kohelet Rabbah (supplied פ״הדי; compare 5:10), “Rabbi Yonatan in the name of Rabbi Yonatan of Beit Guvrin” is, Hyman argues, a scribal error; he proposes “Rabbi Simon in the name of Rabbi Yonatan of Beit Guvrin,” as cited there, 3:2. Seder HaDorot, in his entry, cites that Rabbi Yonatan raised a difficulty

against Rabbi Shimon ben Yakim; Hyman says, with respect, that its author erred in two things. For he means [Jerusalem Talmud Sanhedrin 3:9:22](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Sanhedrin.3.9.22), which reads: “Rabbi Yonatan sat raising a difficulty. Rabbi Yose son of Rabbi Chanina said to him: ‘Here is Shimon ben Yakim.’ The reply was: ‘Let him come up.’” Hyman explains that Rabbi Yose son of Rabbi Chanina intended only to obtain ordination for Rabbi Shimon ben Yakim. Seder HaDorot thought that Rabbi Yonatan raised a difficulty against Rabbi Shimon ben Yakim, but Hyman argues that Shimon was actually among the questioner’s students

and that the questioner ordained him then. (2) Hyman proposes reading Rabbi Yochanan instead of Rabbi Yonatan, citing [Sanhedrin 30b:2-4](https://www.sefaria.org/Sanhedrin.30b.2-4) in support of his view that Rabbi Shimon ben Elyakim and Rabbi Yose son of Rabbi Chanina were students of Rabbi Yochanan.[^11] Hyman continues: Now although Yonatan was like a colleague of Rabbi Chanina and his colleagues, he was much younger than they; therefore we find that Rabbi Yochanan received from all of them and they were counted as his teachers, but Rabbi Yonatan he regarded like a colleague, as we find in [Gittin 78b:5](https://www.sefaria.org/Gittin.78b.5) and [Chullin 45a:10](https://www.sefaria.org/Chullin.45a.10),

where Rabbi Yochanan asked, “Do our Babylonian colleagues know how to explain a reason like this?” Hyman takes this to refer to Rabbi Yonatan. (Rashi explains: Rabbi Yonatan was from Babylonia and went up to the Land of Israel.) Already in Rabbi Yochanan’s youth he was in his company, as in Rosh Hashanah 2:7, where they said that Rabbi Yochanan came in, and he was the youngest of them; they said to him, “Say: Behold the year…” Rabbi Yonatan said: “See the language the son of the smith has taught us,” etc. In Bikkurim 2:4

and Vayikra Rabbah, end of chapter 22, Rabbi Yochanan asked him; and in Berakhot, beginning of chapter 9, both went to the villages of the South. When Rabbi Yochanan was already an old man, Rabbi Yonatan was still alive, as in Terumot 8:4: Rabbi Ami was captured in Sifsifa; Rabbi Yonatan had already given up on him and said, “Let the dead be wrapped in his shroud”; but Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish saved him and told the bandits to come to the old man (Rabbi Yochanan).

In [Gittin 30b:5](https://www.sefaria.org/Gittin.30b.5): a dispute of Rabbi Yonatan and Rabbi Yochanan. He also called Resh Lakish “Master,” in Kohelet Rabbah 3:14. Seder HaDorot cites that Rav Chaviva was his colleague, and this is from the Gemara, [Shabbat 54b](https://www.sefaria.org/Shabbat.54b.20), where they said: “Rav and Rabbi Chanina, Rabbi Yochanan and Rav Chaviva … exchange Rabbi Yochanan and insert Rabbi Yonatan”; but Hyman writes: I have already explained in the entry Rav Chaviva that he did not live in their time. In [Yevamot 86b:4](https://www.sefaria.org/Yevamot.86b.4): “It was stated … Rabbi

Yonatan and the elders (סביא) disagree about it.” Most of his sayings remain to us through his distinguished student Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani, or as he is called in the Jerusalem Talmud, Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachman; in the Babylonian Talmud they are mostly in aggadah, and in the Jerusalem Talmud mostly in halakhah. Likewise his conduct is related in [Yoma 9b:5](https://www.sefaria.org/Yoma.9b.5): “Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani said: When Rabbi Yonatan reached this verse,

he wept”; and [Yoma 22b:5-6](https://www.sefaria.org/Yoma.22b.5-6): “Rabbi Yonatan raised a contradiction (רמי).” In [Pesachim 24a:3-4](https://www.sefaria.org/Pesachim.24a.3-4) and [Bava Batra 123a:12-13](https://www.sefaria.org/Bava_Batra.123a.12-13) it is stated explicitly that Rabbi Yonatan was his teacher; see the entry Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani. Likewise Rabbi Abba son of Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba spoke in his name in Sanhedrin 2:2 and Vayikra Rabbah (locator supplied as פל״הד״א). Rabbi Abbahu in his name, in Kohelet Rabbah 3:13. Rabbi Binyamin bar Yefet in his name, as in Bereshit Rabbah 43:3,

but Hyman proposes reading there “in the name of Rabbi Yochanan,” as in Tanchuma, Lekh Lekha 11. Rav Dimi brought halakhot in his name, as in [Bava Batra 74b:13](https://www.sefaria.org/Bava_Batra.74b.13)[^12] and [Bava Batra 79a:3](https://www.sefaria.org/Bava_Batra.79a.3) and [Bekhorot 51b:8](https://www.sefaria.org/Bekhorot.51b.8). Rabbi Ze’ira in his name, in Kilayim 5:6 and Ketubot 5:1. Rav Chisda spoke in the name of Rabbi Yonatan in [Bava Kamma 67a:9](https://www.sefaria.org/Bava_Kamma.67a.9). Rabbi Yehudah ben Pazi in his name, as in Shabbat, chapter 4,

beginning of halakhah 2. Rabbi Yaakov bar Acha in his name, as in Maaser Sheni 3:1 and Shabbat 1:4. Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi in his name, as in Shabbat, chapter 4, end of halakhah 2, where he said: “A person should never refrain from going to the study house.” So it is in [Shabbat 83b:10](https://www.sefaria.org/Shabbat.83b.10) in the name of Rabbi Yonatan, but Dikdukei Soferim reads Rabbi Yochanan. Likewise there, at the end of chapter 14: “Rabbi Yaakov bar Acha said in the name of Rabbi

Yonatan: One may heal oneself with anything except idolatry”; in [Pesachim 25a:10](https://www.sefaria.org/Pesachim.25a.10) the saying is in the name of Rabbi Yochanan, as Hyman argues that Rabbi Yaakov bar Acha was Rabbi Yochanan’s student. Menachem in his name, as in Peah 6:4. Rabbi Shmuel bar Ami in his name, as in [Yevamot 105a:13](https://www.sefaria.org/Yevamot.105a.13) and Avodah Zarah 35a, but Hyman proposes reading there Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani.[^13] Rabbi Simlai asked him, Bereshit Rabbah (locator supplied as פמ״טדח); and in the Jerusalem Talmud,[^16]

[Jerusalem Talmud Pesachim 5:3:5](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Pesachim.5.3.5), [it relates] that Rabbi Simlai came to him and asked him to teach him the Book of Genealogies, and he did not want to. In [Pesachim 62b:8](https://www.sefaria.org/Pesachim.62b.8) they read Rabbi Yochanan, and Hyman proposes the Jerusalem Talmud’s reading.[^14] In Kohelet Rabbah 1:8: one of his students fled to the sectarians, and he went after him to rescue him; see there. The book Bikkoret HaTalmud, p. 19, made much of this to its author’s liking, Hyman says, and did not see that also at 7:26 it should read Rabbi Yonatan

and not Rabbi Natan. His precious sayings fill the whole Talmud and the Midrashim, as cited in the book Nachalat Shimoni; but Hyman says its author mixed together Rabbi Yonatan, Rabbi Yoshiyah’s colleague, Rabbi Yonatan, Rabbi Chiyya’s student, and Rabbi Yonatan, Rabbi Yochanan’s student. Hyman considers it very likely that this Yonatan is Rabbi Yonatan ben Elazar, and as explained in his entry, Rabbi Yonatan ben

Elazar was also a student of Rabbi Shimon son of Rabbi Yose ben Lakonya; and he is also once called Rabbi Yonatan ben Elazar of HaBirah; this requires investigation. His mother is mentioned in [Bava Metzia 84b](https://www.sefaria.org/Bava_Metzia.84b.8), where Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani reports what Rabbi Yonatan’s mother heard from the wife of Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon. Of his personal life, Hyman infers that he was wealthy, as is proven in Shabbat 1:4 and Avodah Zarah 3:8,

where he would send gifts to the officials so that his words would be heeded; and in Kohelet Rabbah 1:8, that his hair fell out and he became bald. Hyman thinks he lived in Tiberias. As proof he cites Kohelet Rabbah 3:14, where Rabbi Yonatan meets Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish coming from Chamat Gader, and [Jerusalem Talmud Eruvin 6:4:5](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Eruvin.6.4.5), where Rabbi Chanina and Rabbi Yonatan go up to Chamat Gader. Hyman says that Chamat Gader is known to be near Tiberias,
citing [Megillah 2b:22](https://www.sefaria.org/Megillah.2b.22) and [Jerusalem Talmud Eruvin 5:7:3](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Eruvin.5.7.3).[^15] And there is

notes.text: Whole supplied Hebrew/all22 English line-group units/current+historical notes and reviewer proposals read. Hyman owns the identifications, generations, conjectural emendations, force of always and uncertainty about Yonatan ben Elazar; no identity merge is admitted. The final ויש remains an incomplete ending and is held. Nine returned evidence paragraphs across both entries were raw/meta/selector/hash bound and read whole. Named MidrashRabbah--TE Kohelet5 selector[9][0] contains the two passages at5:10; supplied פ״הדי is preserved alongside this match. The reviewer’s hyphen-to-dalet OCR history is not established. Other run-together locators פל״הד״א/פמ״טדח stay visible rather than asserted conversions. The ordination reading of סמיך/סמכיה corrects generic support; the saved Guggenheimer JT San3:9 has Yonatan asking, YosebarChanina pointing out ShimonbenYakim and the reply let him come up, while its ending speaks of bringing Shimon up. Hyman’s own interpretation seeks Shimon’s ordination and proposes Yochanan for Yonatan. The separately read Davidson San30b paragraphs1–4 instead have ShimonbenElyakim seek ordination for YosebarChanina, before Yochanan. The accounts must not be silently conflated; the actor comparison remains held. Yoma22b has Yonatan raising a contradiction, not a second anonymous speaker. סביא is elders, not a new personal name Savya; the reviewer’s unlocated Yevamot87b claim remains a locator hold, not proof of absence elsewhere. The supplied MaaserSheni3:3 word נתמט remains visible; supplemental Guggenheimer paragraph7 reads נתמנו and fruit came into their possession, not evidence that their fruit ran out. Named Chull45a retains Babylonian colleagues; Hyman’s singular Yonatan interpretation is attributed. Rabbi Simlai asks Yonatan to teach him the BookofGenealogies, not merely study alongside him. Hyman’s polemic against SederHaDorot/NachalatShimoni/BikkoretHaTalmud remains his voice. Digital editions are not printed pixels or correction-history proof.

The previously unlocated Yonatan-and-elders dispute is present at Davidson Yevamot 86b: it concerns why the Levites were penalized regarding tithe. This supersedes the earlier “exact location open” assessment for that named digital edition only. The supplied87b locator, earlier bounded nonmatches, and uncertainty about Hyman’s printed page remain; סביא means the elders and does not name a new sage.

The consulted Yerushalmi Berakhot 2:3 describes Yonatan stepping over a grave. Kohelet Rabbah 9:5 instead describes his garment trailing over the coffin. In the road story at Avodah Zarah 17a, the consulted Davidson text names Chanina alongside Yonatan, where Hyman gives Chiyya. In Ketubot 49b the man kisses Yonatan’s feet and Chanina asks the question. In Yerushalmi Kiddushin 1:7 the man also kisses Yonatan’s feet, and Yannai asks the question. The consulted Yerushalmi Eruvin 6:4 shows both Paras and Natan at Chamat Gader. Hyman proposes Pas and identifies him with Rabbi Afes. Hyman’s account and the earlier note give the Book of Genealogies in the Yonatan episode. In the consulted Yerushalmi Pesachim 5:3, Simlai asks Yonatan to teach him aggadah. In Bavli Pesachim 62b, Simlai asks Yochanan for the Book of Genealogies. The parallel accounts differ in both the teacher and the subject of the request.

The supplied Hebrew reads קים לעיל. Hyman’s printed page 699 and the consulted Yerushalmi Sanhedrin 3:9 read יקום לעיל. In the Yerushalmi, Yonatan raises a question, Yose son of Chanina points out Shimon ben Yakim, and the account ends with Shimon being brought up. The consulted Bavli Sanhedrin 30b instead has Shimon seek ordination for Yose son of Chanina and Yochanan ordain Yose. Hyman takes the Yerushalmi to concern Shimon’s ordination and proposes reading Yochanan for Yonatan. The two passages preserve different roles.

Hyman’s printed locator is Gittin עח;. The exact passage in the consulted edition is on 78b. It and Chullin 45a give the question in the plural, “our Babylonian colleagues,” in response to a teaching transmitted in Yonatan’s name. Hyman understands the reference as pointing to Yonatan.

Hyman’s printed page 700 cites Yevamot 86b (פו:), where the supplied Hebrew has 87b (פז:). The consulted 86b names Rabbi Yonatan and the elders in the dispute about the Levites’ tithe. The passage gives two answers without specifying who gave each one.

Hyman’s printed page 700 cites Jerusalem Talmud Eruvin 5:7, where the supplied Hebrew gives 5:6. The consulted 5:7 discusses the hot springs of Tiberias and gives separate examples involving Magdala and Gadara. Megillah 2b gives the distance from Hamtan to Tiberias. These comparisons leave Yonatan’s residence uncertain. In the inspected print the article ends immediately after ויש (“And there is”), before the next Rabbi Yonatan heading.

[Bekhorot 38b:5–7](https://www.sefaria.org/Bekhorot.38b.5-7) names Rabbah bar bar Chana and Rabbi Yochanan ben Elazar. Hyman proposes Rabbah bar Chana for the first name and reports Rabbi Yonatan for the second from Shitah Mekubbetzet. [Shabbat 54b:20](https://www.sefaria.org/Shabbat.54b.20) specifies the substitution of Rabbi Yonatan for Rabbi Yochanan in the order Moed. [Seder HaDorot 1879](https://www.girsology.com/seder-hadorot.html?entry=1879&lang=en) groups several transmissions under the otherwise unspecified Rabbi Yonatan.

In [Avodah Zarah 17a:17](https://www.sefaria.org/Avodah_Zarah.17a.17), the consulted text names Rabbi Chanina alongside Rabbi Yonatan. The road story continues at [Avodah Zarah 17b:1](https://www.sefaria.org/Avodah_Zarah.17b.1). [Shevuot 18b:4](https://www.sefaria.org/Shevuot.18b.4) names the questioner as Rabbi Yonatan ben Yose ben Lakonya. Hyman treats that attribution as an error.

In [Ketubot 49b:13](https://www.sefaria.org/Ketubot.49b.13), Rabbi Chanina asks about the man kissing Yonatan’s foot. The explanation continues on [Ketubot 50a:1](https://www.sefaria.org/Ketubot.50a.1). In [Jerusalem Talmud Kiddushin 1:7:15](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Kiddushin.1.7.15), Rabbi Yonatan is still the one whose foot is kissed, and Rabbi Yannai asks the question.

The roles differ across the two accounts. In [Jerusalem Talmud Sanhedrin 3:9:22](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Sanhedrin.3.9.22), Yonatan has Shimon brought up after Yose points him out. In [Sanhedrin 30b:2-4](https://www.sefaria.org/Sanhedrin.30b.2-4), Shimon seeks ordination for Yose and Rabbi Yochanan ordains Yose.

Rav Dimi’s transmission about Gabriel and Leviathan begins at [Bava Batra 74b:13](https://www.sefaria.org/Bava_Batra.74b.13) and continues on [Bava Batra 75a:1](https://www.sefaria.org/Bava_Batra.75a.1).

[Yevamot 105a:13](https://www.sefaria.org/Yevamot.105a.13) reads Shmuel bar Ami. The parallel at [Rosh Hashanah 18a:7](https://www.sefaria.org/Rosh_Hashanah.18a.7) gives Shmuel bar Nachmani as an alternate transmission.

In [Jerusalem Talmud Pesachim 5:3:5](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Pesachim.5.3.5), Simlai asks Yonatan to teach him aggadah. In [Pesachim 62b:8](https://www.sefaria.org/Pesachim.62b.8), he asks Yochanan to teach him the Book of Genealogies.

[Megillah 2b:22](https://www.sefaria.org/Megillah.2b.22) measures from Hamtan to Tiberias. [Jerusalem Talmud Eruvin 5:7:3](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Eruvin.5.7.3) discusses the springs of Tiberias and gives Gadara as a separate example.

[Yevamot 105a:13](https://www.sefaria.org/Yevamot.105a.13) names Rav Shmuel bar Ami in Rabbi Yonatan’s name. The parallel at [Rosh Hashanah 18a:7](https://www.sefaria.org/Rosh_Hashanah.18a.7) gives Shmuel bar Nachmani as an alternative. [Avodah Zarah 5a:3-4](https://www.sefaria.org/Avodah_Zarah.5a.3-4) has Shmuel bar Nachmani in Rabbi Yonatan’s name on two other teachings. Hyman cites Avodah Zarah 35a, and the exact passage he intended there remains uncertain.
